title: The spectral norm gives the Banach topology of a reduced affinoid
statement:
Let $K$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field], complete for a nontrivial real-valued nonarchimedean absolute value. A Tate algebra $T_r=K\langle X_1,\ldots,X_rangle$ is the restricted-series ring of [def-trf-restricted-series-presentation], with Gauss norm $\|\sum a_
u X^
u\|_G=\sup_
u|a_
u|$. Let $C
e0$ be a reduced quotient of such an algebra with its affinoid Banach topology. Define $ho(c)=\sup_\chi|\chi(c)|$, where $\chi:C	o K$ runs over continuous unital $K$-algebra homomorphisms. Then $ho$ is a complete nonarchimedean $K$-algebra norm: $ho(c)=0$ iff $c=0$, $ho(1)=1$, $ho(c+d)\le\max(ho(c),ho(d))$, $ho(cd)\leho(c)ho(d)$, and $ho(ac)=|a|ho(c)$ for $a\in K$. It is power-multiplicative: $ho(c^m)=ho(c)^m$ for every $m\ge1$. For any Tate quotient norm $\|\cdot\|_0$ on $C$ there is $M\ge1$ such that $ho(c)\le\|c\|_0\le Mho(c)$ for every $c\in C$.

source.place: BGR Theorem 6.2.4/1 (spectral norm is a Banach norm); compare Conrad, Several approaches to non-archimedean geometry, Theorem 1.2.6(1),(5) and the following paragraph, PDF pp.6–7, read online 2026-10-24. The character formula specializes maximal ideals to K-rational characters because K is algebraically closed. Archival copy WANTED; not present in this checkout.

proof.text: Fix an arbitrary Tate presentation with quotient norm $\|\cdot\|_0$. By [lem-trf-affinoid-quotient-norm-topology] this norm is complete and gives the stated topology. Put $s_C(c)=\sup_{\mathfrak m\in\operatorname{Max}C}|c\bmod\mathfrak m|$. By [lem-trf-affinoid-supremum-seminorm-calculus], every residue field is finite over $K$, hence is $K$ because $K$ is algebraically closed, and $s_C(c)\le\|c\|_0$. The quotient norm has $\|1\|_0\le1$ from the constant lift and $\|1\|_0\ge1$ from nondegeneracy and submultiplicativity. The resulting residue characters are contractive by [lem-per-banach-character-norm-bound], hence continuous. Conversely a unital $K$-algebra map $C\to K$ is onto (it fixes $K$), has maximal kernel and is precisely that kernel's residue character. Thus the two indexing sets agree and $\rho=s_C$, in particular $\rho$ is finite. Nonzero $C$ has a maximal ideal, so this character set is nonempty.

proof.text: Choose $j:C\hookrightarrow B=\prod_{i=1}^s B_i$ and $T_i\hookrightarrow B_i$ by [lem-trf-affinoid-finite-galois-envelope], with their quotient norms $\|\cdot\|_i$. Give $B$ the maximum norm. It is a complete finite $C$-module: coordinatewise limits prove completeness and concatenating finite generating lists proves module finiteness. The bounded maps $j_i$ give $\|cb\|_B\le(\max_i D_i)\|c\|_0\|b\|_B$. Apply [lem-trf-affinoid-finite-module-strictness] to the injective $C$-linear map $j:C\to B$. We get $A>0$ with $\|c\|_0\le A\max_i\|j_i(c)\|_i$. Only this finite inclusion is used; no assertion about closedness of an arbitrary affinoid inclusion is needed.

proof.text:
For each $i$ put $F_i=\operatorname{Frac}(T_i)$ and $L_i=\operatorname{Frac}(B_i)$, and let $n_i=[L_i:F_i]\ge1$. Every element of $L_i$ is $ eta/t$ with $ eta\in B_i$ and $0
e t\in T_i$: for $0
e b'\in B_i$ take an integral equation $b'^r+t_{r-1}b'^{r-1}+\cdots+t_0=0$ over $T_i$ of minimal degree; then $t_0
e0$ since $B_i$ is a domain, and $1/b'=-(b'^{r-1}+\cdots+t_1)/t_0$. Hence $B_i$ spans $L_i$ over $F_i$, and we choose an $F_i$-basis $e_{i1},\ldots,e_{in_i}\in B_i$. By [lem-trf-tate-galois-trace-supremum-bound] the trace $\operatorname{Tr}_{L_i/F_i}(b)$ lies in $T_i$ for every $b\in B_i$; in particular every entry of $G_i=(\operatorname{Tr}(e_{ik}e_{i\ell}))_{k,\ell}$ and every $\operatorname{Tr}(e_{ik}b)$ lies in $T_i$, so $\Phi_i(b)=(\operatorname{Tr}(e_{ik}b))_k$ is a $T_i$-linear map $B_i	o T_i^{n_i}$. Since $L_i/F_i$ is a finite separable field extension, $L_i$ is an étale $F_i$-algebra (a product with one separable factor), so by [lem-sbc-trace-form-nondegenerate-iff-etale-field] the trace form of $L_i/F_i$ is nondegenerate, i.e. $\det G_i
e0$. If $\Phi_i(b)=0$, write $b=\sum_\ell f_\ell e_{i\ell}$ with $f_\ell\in F_i$; then $G_i(f_\ell)_\ell=0$. Multiplying by the adjugate and using $\det G_i
e0$ gives all $f_\ell=0$, so $b=0$.

proof.text: Equip $T_i^{n_i}$ with the maximum Gauss norm; it is complete by [lem-trf-restricted-series-gauss-completion] and coordinatewise limits. The $T_i$-action on $B_i$ is bounded by the constants $E_i$ from step 2 and submultiplicativity. Both modules are finite over the affinoid $T_i$. Apply [lem-trf-affinoid-finite-module-strictness] to $\Phi_i$: there is $H_i>0$ such that $\|b\|_i\le H_i\max_k\|\operatorname{Tr}(e_{ik}b)\|_G$. By [lem-trf-tate-galois-trace-supremum-bound] each coordinate is at most $\rho_{B_i}(e_{ik}b)\le\rho_{B_i}(e_{ik})\rho_{B_i}(b)$; the latter inequality follows by applying multiplicativity in each residue field and taking suprema. Hence $\|b\|_i\le H_i R_i\rho_{B_i}(b)$, where $R_i=\max(1,\max_k\rho_{B_i}(e_{ik}))$ is finite by [lem-trf-affinoid-supremum-seminorm-calculus].

source.place: Theorem 4, PDF pp.2-3, finite-envelope and trace argument; agent assembly with finite-module strictness in place of Lemma 3 for arbitrary inclusions. Read online 2026-10-24; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: For every $j_i:C\to B_i$, [lem-trf-affinoid-supremum-seminorm-calculus] gives $\rho_{B_i}(j_i(c))\le s_C(c)=\rho(c)$. Substitution into steps 2 and 4 yields $\|c\|_0\le A\max_i(H_iR_i)\rho(c)$. Taking $M=\max(1,A\max_i(H_iR_i))$ and combining with step 1 gives $\rho(c)\le\|c\|_0\le M\rho(c)$. In particular $\rho(c)=0$ forces $\|c\|_0=0$, hence $c=0$; the converse holds since every character maps zero to zero. The quotient presentation was arbitrary, so this proves the assertion for every Tate quotient norm.

source.place: Theorem 4, PDF pp.2-3, finite-envelope and trace argument; agent assembly with finite-module strictness in place of Lemma 3 for arbitrary inclusions. Read online 2026-10-24; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: For every character $\chi$, $|\chi(1)|=1$, $|\chi(c+d)|\le\max(|\chi(c)|,|\chi(d)|)$, $|\chi(cd)|=|\chi(c)||\chi(d)|$ and $|\chi(ac)|=|a||\chi(c)|$. Taking suprema in the nonempty bounded character family gives respectively $\rho(1)=1$, the ultrametric inequality, submultiplicativity, and scalar homogeneity (for $a=0$ both sides are zero). Also $\rho(-c)=\rho(c)$. The positive-power identity $\rho(c^m)=\rho(c)^m$ follows directly from the positive-power identity for $s_C$ in [lem-trf-affinoid-supremum-seminorm-calculus], since step 1 identified these functions.

source.place: Theorem 4, PDF pp.2-3, finite-envelope and trace argument; agent assembly with finite-module strictness in place of Lemma 3 for arbitrary inclusions. Read online 2026-10-24; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: If $(c_n)$ is $\rho$-Cauchy, the upper inequality $\|c_n-c_m\|_0\le M\rho(c_n-c_m)$ makes it $\|\cdot\|_0$-Cauchy. Completeness of the quotient norm from step 1 gives $c\in C$ with $\|c_n-c\|_0\to0$. The lower inequality $\rho(c_n-c)\le\|c_n-c\|_0$ gives convergence for $\rho$. Thus the norm is complete. The same inequalities show equality of the two topologies by their metric balls, so this is the affinoid Banach topology.
